summary: Revises the Telnet STATUS option, which lets one side ask the other about the state of its Telnet options. It was replaced by RFC 859.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 651 revises the Telnet STATUS option so one side can ask how the other side sees current option settings without renegotiating each option. The endpoints use DO and WILL to permit status exchanges, then SEND and IS subcommands to request and report the state; RFC 859 later obsoleted this memo.

subtitle: A revision of the Telnet STATUS option for asking about current option settings.

tldr.problem: Simply renegotiating Telnet options to learn their state could lead to nonterminating request loops.
tldr.mechanism: The STATUS option uses DO and WILL to permit discussion, then SEND and IS subcommands to request and report option state.

sections.title: The Telnet STATUS Option
sections.content:
STATUS is Telnet option 5. It lets a user or process verify the current status of options, such as echoing, as seen by the other end. By default, each side uses DON'T STATUS or WON'T STATUS, so the option status is not discussed.

The revision places the actual status exchange in subnegotiation, which fits the normal structure of Telnet options and avoids using option renegotiation just to inspect current state.
sections.plainLanguage: STATUS lets one end ask what settings the other end currently believes are in effect. The default is not to exchange this information.

sections.title: Permission and Status Requests
sections.content:
DO STATUS means the sender wants to send status requests or confirms it is willing to send them. WILL STATUS means the sender agrees to provide status, either spontaneously or in response to a request. These commands grant permission for later discussion; the actual status information is sent in subcommands.

Only the sender of DO may send IAC SB STATUS SEND IAC SE, where SEND is code 1. Only the sender of WILL may send IAC SB STATUS IS ... IAC SE, where IS is code 0. The WILL side may send status without a request, so a request can result in duplicate reports at worst.
sections.plainLanguage: First the endpoints agree that status information may be exchanged. The DO side can request a report, and the WILL side sends the report.

sections.title: Reading an IS Report
sections.content:
An IS report uses WILL, DO, and SB entries in the same way as ordinary Telnet option negotiation. In this report, SB is terminated by SE rather than IAC SE. To send an SE byte as ordinary data, the byte is doubled.

Options not explicitly described in the report are assumed to be in their default states, so one IS subcommand describes the condition of all options.
sections.plainLanguage: The IS report lists options that are not in their default state. Any option it leaves out is assumed to be at its default setting.
